# Bootcamp
A lot in a short time, with an intense focus. Concepts, practical advice and hands-on coding.

Build and run your first cluster on your laptop, then a whistle-stop tour of the essentials.

No previous Hazelcast experience required.

Should use Java 8, and an IDE such as Eclipse or Intellij.

The examples are in Maven, but would not be difficult to convert to Gradle. Gradle users usually can figure out Maven, less frequently the reverse.

## NOTE 1
Maven builds executable Jar files, so you need to run as far as the _package_ phase. So try "*mvn install*".

## Note 2
A lot, but not enough time for everything.# Bootcamp labs

4 labs showing some features

## Lab 1
Uses Hazelcast only with server JVMs, known as "_embedded_" mode. Your application contains the Hazelcast cluster.

Some options demonstrate how clusters join together.

Basic data structures are shown -- maps, queues, topics & atomics. These are distributed on the cluster so
as resilient as you configure them to be.

## Lab 2
Uses Hazelcast in client-server mode. The cluster is the server JVMs acting collectively. Clients don't host data.

This example is mainly about grid operations, running processing *distributed* on the grid. Rather than pull
the data back to the client to modify and safe, instead runnables, callables and entry processors run on
one or more servers at the request of a client.

## Lab 3
Client-server again, but now for Spring users.

Use Hazelcast from Spring, in the usual @Bean style.

Or, use Hazelcast as an implementation of JRS107, the Java Caching Standard. Although the implementation
is Hazelcast (obviously!), calls are to a caching provider so agnostic of the implementation provider.

## Lab 4
A client-server example using Spring Data for Hazelcast.

The server uses Spring Boot to create a Hazelcast for minimal code.

The client is Spring, a Spring @Repository is used to retrieve data, much the same as any other Spring @Repository.

## NOTE 1
Maven builds executable Jar files, so you need to run as far as the _package_ phase. So try "*mvn install*".

## NOTE 2
If something doesn't work quite as expected, that's when you learn the most.

# Bootcamp lab4

## Objective
Use Spring-Data-Hazelcast for resilient data access in a familiar Spring like way,
no knowledge of Hazelcast is really needed.

## Step 1 - cluster formation
Start a couple of instances of the server. The first to start will load some test data.

## Step 2 - Spring client
Run the Spring client.

All Hazelcast plumbing is encapsulated in `HazelcastSpringConfiguration`. Everything
else is normal Spring, use of @Service and @Repository.

Note in the @Repository how methods are defined and Spring deduces the implementation.
Add some more if you like.

## Step 3 - resilience
Kill a server and re-run a client. A Spring developer gets resilience!

# Bootcamp lab6

## Objective
A "Hello World" for a simple GET REST API, using Spring Boot.

This lab doesn't use Hazelcast directly. It shows the smallest possible REST service,
which is a good starting point for exposing Hazelcast data over HTTP.

## Step 1 - build
From the `bootcamp` directory, build as usual. Maven builds an executable Jar, so you need
to run as far as the _package_ phase.

```
mvn install
```

## Step 2 - run the server
Either run `SpringBootServer` from your IDE, or from the command line:

```
java -jar labs/lab6/lab6-server/target/bootcamp-lab6-server.jar
```

The server listens on port 8080. Change `server.port` in `application.yml` if this is in use.

## Step 3 - call the API
`HelloController` has two GET endpoints. Try them with curl or a browser.

```
curl http://localhost:8080/hello
Hello, World!

curl http://localhost:8080/hello/Hazelcast
Hello, Hazelcast!
```

## Step 4 - extend it
Add another `@GetMapping` method to `HelloController`, perhaps one that takes a
request parameter (`@RequestParam`), or returns a JSON object instead of plain text.
EOF

text: out as the other labs. It

I added the new lab as `bootcamp/labs/lab6`, a Spring Boot "Hello World" GET API. I couldn't build or run it because Java and Maven aren't installed here. It follows the same pom and Spring Boot setup as `lab4-server`, so it should build with `mvn install` from `bootcamp/`, but that is untested.

- **Code:** `HelloController` has two endpoints, `GET /hello` returning `Hello, World!` and `GET /hello/{name}` returning `Hello, <name>!`. `SpringBootServer` starts the app on port 8080, set in `application.yml`.
- **Docs:** `lab6/README.md` has the same Objective/Step layout as the other labs. It covers building, running from an IDE or with `java -jar labs/lab6/lab6-server/target/bootcamp-lab6-server.jar`, `curl` examples, and an "extend it" exercise.
- **Registration:** I added `<module>lab6</module>` to `bootcamp/labs/pom.xml`. I also added a Lab 6 section to `bootcamp/labs/README.md` and changed its count from "4 labs" to "6 labs".
- **Dependencies:** Like every bootcamp module, it inherits `hazelcast-enterprise` from the parent pom, so the build needs the private Hazelcast repository. The lab itself doesn't use Hazelcast.
- **Lab 5:** It exists but has no section in `labs/README.md`. I left that alone as unrelated, so the README now jumps from Lab 4 to Lab 6.
